title: Being Salt and Light in Secular Places
summary: Small choices of honesty and faithfulness in daily tasks shape character and build trust with others.
author: Nora Achieng'
contentHtml:
Matthew 5:13–14 “You are the salt of the earth… You are the light of the world.”


I was reflecting on the words of Jesus when He called us the “salt of the earth” and the “light of the world.” These two metaphors are not decorative, they are functional. Salt preserves and flavors. Light guides and reveals. Jesus wasn’t asking us to merely exist in the world; He was inviting us to influence it.


But influence is rarely easy, especially in secular spaces. Whether in the workplace, in schools, or even in boardrooms, living out faith with integrity often collides with pressure, competition, and compromise. Yet this is precisely where we are called to shine. Our value is not just in what we believe privately but in how that belief flavors and illuminates the environments we step into.


When I think about salt, I remember Joseph in Egypt (Genesis 41). A Hebrew slave, betrayed by his own brothers, he found himself in Pharaoh’s court…a deeply secular space. Did he compromise his faith? No. Instead, he offered wisdom, integrity, and excellence. His presence preserved a nation in famine and pointed an entire empire toward the God of heaven. Joseph was salt.


When I think about light, I remember Daniel in Babylon (Daniel 6). Surrounded by idol worship and political corruption, he still prayed faithfully and refused to bow to compromise. His light exposed the futility of false gods and revealed the greatness of Yahweh. Daniel’s light could not be hidden; it shaped kings and kingdoms. That is what being light means.


The two remind me that being salt and light is not about withdrawing from secular spaces but about transforming them. It’s not about carrying a Bible in every meeting, but about letting the Word shape the way we speak, act, and treat people.


From my little experience, I’ve learned that true influence is not achieved through loud speeches or heated debates. It often takes root in quiet consistency, attentive listening, and genuine care for others. Dale Carnegie, in his classic How to Win Friends and Influence People, affirms this principle, reminding us that people are not won by arguments but by feeling truly heard and valued. At its heart, influence begins with empathy—and I believe empathy is one of the purest expressions of faith, a living act of love.


I recently subscribed to the China Christian Daily blog, and I was struck by an article that spoke on the very same subject.


“Recently, I attended a meeting where I came into contact with a workplace group. The members were mostly in their thirties and forties, representing the backbone of workplace ministry in the church. When discussing workplace ministry, three believers shared their testimonies and perspectives.


A Christian woman surnamed Wang, who works in the education sector, believes: ‘In the current environment, it’s difficult to evangelize through traditional church methods. In the past, staff workers could organize street evangelism or distribute gospel tracts, but that no longer works. So, I hope the church will place more emphasis on workplace evangelism and provide us with the necessary training and pastoral care.’


A male believer with the surname of Tan, who leads a workplace group, shared that workplace Christians often interact with many non-believers from diverse backgrounds. In this vast field, each believer can be the light and salt for the Lord. However, after observing many cases, Tan said: ‘Workplace ministry isn’t just about enthusiasm for evangelism. The most important thing is to do your job well first with honesty and dedication. Otherwise, the more you evangelize, the fewer people will believe.’” (China Christian Daily: October, 2024)


Being salt and light is not about perfection. It is about presence. Salt loses its power if it never touches food. Light loses its meaning if it’s hidden under a basket. In the same way, our faith must step into real-world conversations, workplaces, and relationships. Not to condemn, but to preserve. Not to blind, but to illuminate.


Jesus didn’t call us the salt and light of the church. He called us the salt and light of the world. That means our greatest testimonies may not always be in pulpits, but in classrooms, offices, markets, and even social media platforms. Every time we choose honesty over shortcuts, kindness over harshness, and service over self-promotion, we flavor and illuminate the spaces we occupy.


As I grow in this journey, I am convinced that influence is not measured by the crowd that applauds you but by the quiet lives you impact. Being salt and light means living in such a way that others are preserved from decay and guided out of darkness, not by force, but by love.


This is my encouragement today: Wherever God has placed you, in secular or sacred spaces, shine faithfully. Do not dilute your salt. Do not dim your light. Be the quiet influence, the steady presence, the living testimony. For when Jesus called us salt and light, He was not giving us an option. He was describing our identity. And the world needs us to live it out.

title: Receipts of Righteousness
summary: Faithfulness to God builds a bold record before heaven that can speak for you in times of need.
author: Nora Achieng
contentHtml:
Living with Spiritual Receipts


2 Kings 20:3 (KJV)
"I beseech thee, O Lord, remember now how I have walked before thee in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done that which is good in thy sight. And Hezekiah wept sore."

Have you ever kept a receipt as proof of a purchase, so that when there’s an issue, you have a reference to defend your claim?

When you buy something special from the store, you will ensure that the receipt is well kept. If in any case come a problem with that which you had bought, at least you will go and show evidence that you were given this and now there is a problem…we've had cases of evidence provision so many times

In life, receipts prove that a transaction occurred. In the spiritual realm, your faithfulness becomes your receipt a record of your walk with God. It’s not about manipulation; it’s about relational boldness. That at the point of darkness, where your death is being declared, you can turn to God and say:

“Lord, remember how I have walked before you…”

What kind of boldness that would be? Can a man really ask God to remember his obedience and use it as a basis for deliverance?

Yes. Because faithfulness has a voice. After winning trust from someone… think of that courage…that is what faithfulness does.

There comes a time in every believer's life when all the prayers, fasting, service, obedience, and secret tears must speak not to people, not to the church but directly to God…ttimes when you are pressed in a corner, where the only thing you can present is the life you’ve lived before the Lord. In such times, your faithfulness becomes your defense your evidence. And just like in the world, when you need to make a claim, you present a receipt. That’s what this message is about: spiritual receipts...a life of righteous devotion to God that gives you confidence to call upon Him boldly in crisis.

2 Kings 20…In 2 Kings 20, the prophet Isaiah comes with a terrifying message: "Set your house in order; for you shall die, and not live."

King Hezekiah gives us a remarkable example. The prophet Isaiah walks into his palace with a chilling prophecy: “Set your house in order, for you shall die and not live.”

I was thinking if I was Hezekiah, next was to start repenting, especially when your ways are not straight. But to them who have banked their spiritual wealth in God, they demand it back at the time of need…like here

There’s no hope, no condition, no warning,just a death sentence. But what Hezekiah does next is what many of us would never dare:

But Hezekiah doesn’t panic. He doesn’t question Isaiah. He turns to the wall and prays. He knows how to handle things of God…he knows there is something he has somewhere…God remember.

“I beseech thee, O Lord, remember now how I have walked before thee in truth…”

He turns his face to the wall, weeps, and prays, “Lord, remember how I’ve walked with You… how I’ve served You… how I’ve done what is right in Your sight.” He holds up his receipt.

Hezekiah doesn't pray out of fear; he prays out of covenant boldness. Because He is sure. He doesn’t remind God of His power, He reminds Him of their relationship. The trust they have built. And God responds. Before Isaiah even leaves the palace courtyard, the Lord sends him back with a new message: “I’ve heard your prayer. I’ve seen your tears. I will heal you.” What changed? The receipt,Hezekiah’s faithfulness,spoke.

In 2 Kings 20, the prophet Isaiah comes with a terrifying message: "Set your house in order; for you shall die, and not live."

That prayer wasn’t filled with flattery or excuses,it was filled with receipts. He had lived right. He had served faithfully. He had restored worship in Judah. He had been a righteous king in a dark time.

God answered not with silence but with reversal. Isaiah hadn’t even left the palace when the word of the Lord came back: "I have heard your prayer, I have seen your tears: behold, I will heal you..." (v.5)

This tells us something profound:

Heaven responds to righteousness.

This story isn’t about earning miracles through works. It’s about what relational loyalty looks like. We all know people who, because of the trust they’ve built over time, can ask things from us that others can’t. That’s not manipulation; that’s loyalty honored. Likewise, when you’ve been consistent with God walking in truth, tithing faithfully, praying sincerely, serving humbly there are moments when those acts speak louder than your words.

Hebrews 6:10 says:

“God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labor of love...”

Some believers struggle with this idea because it sounds like we are trying to “earn” God’s favor. But no! This isn’t about merit; it’s about relational equity.

Just like a faithful employee gains the trust of their boss, a faithful Christian builds a walk with God that can be leaned on in the day of crisis.

Faithful giving, praying, serving, standing for truth...these are recorded in heaven. When the crisis comes, these become receipts of righteousness.

Let see what God is saying about Job…

Job 1:8…my servant

When Satan accused him before God, the Lord didn’t need to search his record. He already had it. “Have you considered my servant Job?

My servant, wow…there must have been some special divine connection in this relationship.

There is none like him.” That’s what it means to live in a way that heaven can vouch for you. Job didn’t need to plead his case; God Himself had the receipts.

“There is none like him in the earth, a perfect and an upright man...” (Job 1:8)

God had the receipt on Job. His records…That is what happens when our relationship with heavens is faithfully manned.

The scene at the plain of Dura – Daniel 3-

In Daniel 3, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego stood before King Nebuchadnezzar facing the fiery furnace. What gave them the courage to say, “Our God whom we serve is able to deliver us”? They had receipts. They had served God with integrity, and when it came to the fire, they knew heaven wouldn’t abandon them.

They didn’t plead for mercy in the fire; they simply said“Our God whom we serve is able...”

Their faithful service gave them the confidence to face death.

Receipts of faithfulness became insurance in the fire.

Let’s bring it home.

If the Lord were to send a message like He sent to Hezekiah, could you turn to the wall and pray with that kind of boldness?

If the Lord were to tell you, like Hezekiah, “Set your house in order,” could you boldly turn to the wall and say, “Lord, You know how I’ve walked with You”? Would your past obedience be enough to build a case for divine intervention?

This is not spiritual pride. It is covenantal confidence. Isaiah 43:26 says, “Put Me in remembrance. Let us plead together. Declare thou, that thou mayest be justified.” God is inviting us to come boldly...not empty-handed, but with a testimony of walking with Him. You don’t command God in arrogance; you plead with Him based on the relationship you’ve built.

It’s not about perfection,it’s about consistency and covenant.

Faithfulness builds confidence. Faithfulness becomes your evidence.

Some people try to make withdrawals from accounts they’ve never deposited into. Spiritually, you must build your account through prayer, purity, giving, forgiveness, and worship. These are the invisible receipts of righteousness. When you live like this, you gain heaven’s attention. Hebrews 6:10 assures us, “God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labor of love.” In other words, your spiritual sacrifices are being recorded. You are not forgotten.

Consider the woman with the alabaster box. She broke open a year’s worth of wages in oil at Jesus’ feet. Others mocked her, but Jesus said, and it is recorded in John “Wherever the gospel is preached, what this woman has done will be told as a memorial to her.” That was a receipt. And it outlived her.

We must stop living casually and start living covenantally. When crisis comes and it will...it will not be your loud prayers or long fasts that move heaven most. It will be your record. How you’ve walked in the ordinary seasons. Did you trust when no one was watching? Did you forgive when it hurt? Did you tithe even when it was hard? Did you obey when it cost you?

In even the courtroom of heaven, your faithfulness becomes your defense.

That’s why this message is not just an encouragement it's a challenge. Live with receipts. Live so that when the storm comes, your tears don’t speak alone your life does. Live so that, like Hezekiah, you can turn your face to the wall and say, “Lord, You know me. I’ve walked with You. I’ve served You. Please, remember.”

And the God who sees in secret, the God who keeps records, the God who rewards the faithful, will answer.

Extra Thought….

Can God Really Owe a Man?

This is a bold question. But listen to what the Word says:

Isaiah 45:11 (KJV)

There is this wonderful verse in the bible, that is the book of Isaiah…command ye me…

“Concerning the work of my hands, command ye me.”

God isn’t intimidated by our boldness when it’s rooted in obedience. He is pleased when we take His Word seriously enough to say:

“Lord, You said so I stand on it!” “Lord, I’ve walked with You, remember me!”

That’s what Hannah did. That’s what Nehemiah did. That’s what Elijah did.

Receipts of righteousness are heaven’s reminders that you’ve partnered with God,and now you’re making a demand based on that partnership.

Today, He is calling you back to covenant. Back to consistent prayer. Back to sacrificial giving. Back to holy living. Back to your first love. Don’t wait for crisis to start building. Start now. Fill your life with evidence that testifies of your walk with God.

When your day of crisis comes, may heaven look into your life and say, “Yes… they’ve walked with Me. I will intervene.”

As we close, we sing the song that reflects this message: “Great is Thy Faithfulness”...but may it also reflect your life. May your own faithfulness rise as a memorial before God.

So, go and live a life of spiritual receipts. Not so you can boast in yourself...but so that in the hour of need, you can turn to the wall and say, “Lord, remember…”

And He will.

title: The Rest That Welcomes Us Home
summary: Have you ever thought of Sabbath not just as a command, but as God’s first invitation to communion and rest with us?
author: Nora Achieng
contentHtml:
A Heartfelt Prelude


I sit here on this Friday, September 5, 2025 preparation day, feeling the weight of the week’s noise and burdens lift. There’s a sacred invitation waiting for me: tomorrow is Sabbath. And in my soul, I hear a gentle whisper, “Come, rest.”

Have you ever paused, as I am pausing now, to wonder why God created a day of rest? Imagine the Creator, having formed light and darkness, sky and seas, land and life…and He crowns all His work, not with exhaustion, but with rest. “On the seventh day God finished His work… and rested… and made it holy” (Genesis 2:2–3). That rest wasn’t born of weariness—it was the flourish, the invitation, the beginning of communion.

Sabbath Was Made for Us

Friends, the Sabbath is not an archaic rule, nor a burden to bear. Jesus gently reminds us, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. Therefore the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27–28) (GotQuestions.org, Life, Hope & Truth).

Think: God designed this sacred day for us; to bless, uphold, and refresh our hearts.

I often pause to imagine the beauty of creation’s story. God spoke the heavens into place, formed the earth, filled the seas, and breathed life into every living thing. And then, He crowned His work by creating man. But what strikes me most is this: the very first gift He gave humanity was not work, not instruction, but communion—rest. What I like to call the Sabbath rest.

Think of it, friends. Imagine arriving at a grand celebration. The host himself takes you by the hand, not leaving you wandering around unsure, but leading you straight into the heart of the occasion. You are welcomed, honored, made to feel at home. That is what the Sabbath feels like to me. God, the Author of time, invited humanity right into fellowship with Him from the very beginning.

I remember my first time being invited to a special event. The moment I stepped in, the warmth of the welcome filled me with courage and strength for the whole day. That same feeling mirrors what God intended through the Sabbath: a holy welcome, a day that steadies the soul and refreshes the heart.

The Scriptures remind us clearly: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy” (Exodus 20:8). I often ask myself, why “remember”? Because Sabbath is not an ordinary day—it is a divine connection, a sacred bridge to my Savior. After spending the week carrying the cares of the workplace, the worries of family matters, and the endless noise of life, Sabbath becomes my sanctuary. It is the day I cool my heart, release my burdens, and open my soul to drink from the fountain of everlasting knowledge.

For me, the Sabbath is more than a command, it is a story of love, an invitation into communion, and a reminder that my Creator longs for fellowship with me.

Rest for div, Mind, and Soul

In Exodus, the commandment rings clear: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy… For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth… and rested on the seventh day. Therefore the Lord blessed the Sabbath day and made it holy” (Exodus 20:8–11). It’s not just about ceasing work, Sabbath is about setting apart time to dwell with Him.

…Israel is to remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy (Ex. 20:8). The Lord had already begun to form the people’s life in the rhythm of working for six days(Ex. 20:9) and resting on the seventh day as a Sabbath (Ex. 20:10) through the instructions for collecting manna (see Ex. 16:22–26). Here the command is grounded further in the way that it imitates the Lord’s pattern in creation (Ex. 20:11; see Gen. 2:1–3). Every aspect of Israel’s life is to reflect that the people belong to the Lord and are sustained by his hand. The weekly pattern of work and rest is to be a regular and essential part of this (see Ex. 31:12–18). In Deut. 5:15, Moses gives another reason for observing the day: it recalls their redemption from slavery in Egypt.(Crossway April,2025)

This day reframes life’s worries—whether from workplace stress, family anxieties, or global chaos. I lay them down. I slow down. I open my heart, cooled by His love, ready to drink from the fountain of everlasting knowledge. Sabbath is spiritual oxygen.

The prophet Isaiah calls us to “call the Sabbath a delight” (Isaiah 58:13).

A Story of Sabbath Peace

“My parents grew up as nonbelievers in Russia, so when we were baptized in 1992, we were converts not only to the Church but also to Christianity. We understood that joining the Church would change our beliefs as well as our attitudes and our very lives. One source of that change was the commandment to keep the Sabbath day holy, which was totally new to us.

At the time of my family’s conversion, some Church members in Moscow were from other countries and were living in the city as employees of their governments or of private businesses. These members were our walking manuals; it was by being around them that I learned what Church members should do to please the Lord. My best friend then was a Latter-day Saint named David Matthews, who was a teenager like me. Whenever I visited his family on Sundays, I could tell it was a special day. I remember how quiet their house was on that day. They had many children in their family, and during the week all kinds of sounds could usually be heard in their home. But not on Sunday. The children behaved differently, and not because they had to but because they wanted to. I felt the same spirit in David’s home that I felt when priesthood holders administered the sacrament in church.

A few years later I finally learned where this spirit of Sabbath peace and worship came from. During a trip to St. Petersburg that I took with some other Church members, I was discussing with one of my friends, Rebekah Nielson, our plans for the coming day, which was Sunday. Of course our plan would include going to the local branch to participate in Sunday meetings. “Then,” Rebekah said, “we will come back to the place we are staying and will have a quiet and peaceful Sabbath.” She said this with reverence and devotion, and I could feel her love for our Father in Heaven and His Son, Jesus Christ. Sabbath observance was a commandment that was written on the tables of her heart (see 2 Cor. 3:3).

And so it happened. After returning from the branch meetings, the group of us sat together and talked about the things of our souls. We read the scriptures together; we talked about things we were grateful for. We spent the day with “thanksgiving, with cheerful hearts and countenances” (D&C 59:15). I felt the same spirit I had felt in the home of the Matthews family. It was the Spirit of the Lord, which spoke peace to our minds (see D&C 6:23).

I shall never forget that special Sabbath day when I learned that it is not only the letter of the law but also the spirit that makes the day holy. It changed my whole view of that day of the week. Now I knew that the only true source of rest was Jesus Christ Himself. Only in Him could I find enough strength for the week ahead. Since then the Sabbath has become a day of my Lord, or, in other words, a day when my joy can be full.” — Ivan Makarov, Severo-Zamoskvoretsky Branch, Moscow Russia North District

A Call to Sabbath Worship and Fellowship

As part of Advent Band’s spiritual outreach and discipleship, through Bible studies, prayer networks, and care teams we believe deeply in true worship rooted in Sabbath devotion. We envision Sabbath not as a ritual, but as a fresh invitation to fellowship with our Savior.

This day must be special. It’s the day I breathe in grace, I pause from ambition, and I lean into God’s sustaining arms. It connects me back to creation, to redemption, to hope. Sabbath whispers: “You are not a slave to toil. I made you. I love you. Rest.”

Let us make Sabbath worship a sacred call — a day of genuine devotion not driven by obligation, but by delight. Let us come as humble guests, welcomed richly, to the feast of divine rest.

An Invitation to Others

I invite you, dear reader, to prepare your heart today for Sabbath rest tomorrow. Imagine entering a place of belonging. Take the cares off your shoulders. Embrace communion with your Creator. Let Sabbath not be a day of legal burden but a holy delight and a gift crafted lovingly for you.

May your soul be refreshed as you tarry in His presence. May this day become your sanctuary — a place of sweet fellowship, wonder, worship, and rest.

Key Scriptures at a glance

  • Genesis 2:2–3 — God rested, blessed, and made the seventh day holy.
  • Exodus 20:8–11 — Remember the Sabbath, for in six days He made the world and rested on the seventh.
  • Mark 2:27–28 — Sabbath made for man, not man for the Sabbath; Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath.
Editor: Nora Achieng'  |  Friday Sep 5, 2025
